title: ML is reshaping institutional investment industry
claim: Machine learning algorithms outperform human investors by analyzing vast datasets to identify patterns and anomalies.
mechanism: Computational advantage in pattern recognition and systematic execution
validation: Measurable against out-of-sample returns; requires live trading performance or independent institutional benchmarks

title: Alternative data signal quality depends on timeliness and signal-to-noise ratio
claim: Alternative data sources vary dramatically in quality; evaluation requires assessment of signal content quality, data quality, and technical delivery capability.
mechanism: Signal-to-noise and data freshness directly impact predictive power
assumptions: Signal is stationary across time periods
validation: Can be validated by comparing out-of-sample signal decay vs baseline

title: Alpha factors decay over time; signal strength must be continually re-evaluated
claim: Engineered alpha factors based on historical patterns tend to lose predictive power as markets adapt and competitive landscapes shift.

source.section: Engineering alpha factors that predict returns

mechanism: Arbitrage and competition erode alpha; factors become crowded
validation: Out-of-sample factor performance can be tracked over rolling windows; walk-forward testing with regular re-estimation

title: Use Alphalens library to quantify factor predictive performance
claim: The Alphalens library provides standardized metrics (IC, factor quantile returns, turnover) to evaluate signal quality before deployment.

source.section: Separating signal from noise with Alphalens

support: Library explicitly designed for this purpose
mechanism: Quantile binning + forward-return analysis reveals signal/noise
validation: Can be implemented as standard pre-deployment validation; compare Alphalens metrics to out-of-sample performance

title: Mean-variance optimization assumes normal returns; fat tails create downside risk
claim: Classical portfolio optimization is sensitive to assumption violations; extreme events (fat tails) occur more frequently in markets than normal distributions predict.

source.section: How to manage portfolio risk and return

support: Statistical anomaly widely recognized in finance
mechanism: Extreme events not modeled → underestimated tail risk
validation: Compare portfolio drawdowns to VaR predictions; stress testing and EVT analysis

title: Risk parity and hierarchical risk parity for tail-robust allocation
claim: Risk parity and hierarchical risk parity methods reduce reliance on mean-variance assumptions and provide more robust portfolio construction.
support: Methodological innovation described with worked example
mechanism: Risk budgeting per asset/cluster reduces concentration risk
validation: Backtest comparison with mean-variance on out-of-sample data; sensitivity analysis to correlation/volatility changes

title: Cross-validation in finance requires careful time-series splitting
claim: Naive cross-validation (random folds) on time-series data leads to data leakage. Time-series CV must respect temporal ordering and avoid look-ahead bias.
mechanism: Future information leaks into training if folds are random
validation: Compare random vs. time-series CV on holdout test set; walk-forward testing must show no advantage from random CV

title: Look-ahead bias: using future data invalidates backtest results
claim: Look-ahead bias emerges when trading rules use historical information before it was available. Common causes: failure to account for restatements, stock splits, asynchronous EPS/price data.

source.section: Getting the data right - Look-ahead bias

validation: Audit data timestamps against official release dates; rerun backtest with conservative lag assumptions

title: Survivorship bias: excluding dead/delisted securities inflates returns
claim: Backtest data containing only currently-active securities omits bankruptcies, delistings, acquisitions. These failures are disproportionately represented in poor performers.

source.section: Getting the data right - Survivorship bias

mechanism: Dead securities disappear from dataset → portfolio return overstated
validation: Compare returns with/without delisted securities; use historical constituent lists; verify against exchange records

title: Outlier treatment: excluding realistic extremes biases downside risk
claim: Data preparation (winsorizing, clipping) can remove extreme but realistic market values. Fat-tailed distributions show extreme events more frequently than normal distributions predict.

source.section: Getting the data right - Outlier control

failure_modes: Unmodeled tail events in live trading
validation: Compare historical return distributions (empirical vs. Gaussian); stress-test portfolio against historical extremes

title: Sample period selection must include relevant market regimes
claim: Backtests using unrepresentative sample periods (lacking volatility spikes, volume changes, or regime shifts) will not generalize to future market conditions.

source.section: Getting the data right - Sample period

mechanism: Backtest reflects training regime only; new regimes cause failure
assumptions: Future regimes are somewhat represented in history
validation: Benchmark performance across different market regimes (rolling windows); out-of-sample performance degradation analysis

title: Vectorized vs. event-driven backtesting trade off speed for realism
claim: Vectorized backtesting (NumPy/Pandas) is fast but assumes unrealistic execution (all fills at bar-end price). Event-driven engines simulate realistic slippage, partial fills, latency.
mechanism: Vectorized misses microstructure; event-driven is more realistic
failure_modes: Vectorized results don't match live execution
validation: Compare backtest results with out-of-sample live returns; measure realistic slippage vs. backtest assumptions

title: Random forests reduce overfitting through bootstrap aggregation and feature randomness
claim: Ensemble methods (bootstrap aggregation, feature subsampling) reduce overfitting and improve generalization compared to single decision trees.
mechanism: Bagging reduces variance; feature randomness prevents tree correlation
validation: OOB error estimation; cross-validation comparison; compare RF to single tree on out-of-sample test set

title: Out-of-bag (OOB) testing provides unbiased error estimation without holdout
claim: Random forests provide OOB error estimates (samples not in a particular bootstrap) that approximate test error without requiring explicit holdout sets.
mechanism: Each tree trained on ~63% of data; remaining 37% serve as holdout
assumptions: Sufficient trees for stable OOB estimate
validation: Compare OOB error to explicit test set; validate assumption on financial time-series (may violate IID)

title: Gradient boosting (XGBoost/LightGBM) often outperforms random forests on structured tabular data
claim: Gradient boosting machines (XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost) achieve better predictive performance than random forests on many tabular datasets through sequential error correction.
support: Empirical comparison; author emphasis on algorithmic advances
mechanism: Sequential fitting to residuals; adaptive learning rates; early stopping
validation: Empirical comparison on holdout test set; walk-forward cross-validation with proper time-series splitting

title: Feature importance from GBM can guide trading signal design
claim: Gradient boosting models provide feature importance metrics that reveal which factors drive model predictions, enabling more interpretable trading signals.

source.section: Inside the black box - interpreting GBM results

support: Model introspection technique described with examples
mechanism: Gain-based importance shows contribution of each feature to prediction
assumptions: Features are causally related to target
validation: Compare feature importance to domain knowledge; validate stability; walk-forward analysis of feature importance drift

title: Signal quality must be evaluated on out-of-sample data before deployment
claim: Trading signal quality (measured by IC, Sharpe ratio, or confusion matrix) must be validated on data held-out during model training to detect overfitting.
mechanism: OOS data reveals whether model generalizes to new regimes
assumptions: Test data is representative of future
Data is clean and properly split
validation: Empirical comparison of in-sample vs. OOS metrics; walk-forward testing to detect signal decay

title: ML pipeline design should separate research, feature engineering, and backtesting infrastructure
claim: Effective ML4T systems benefit from modular design: data sourcing → feature engineering → signal generation → portfolio construction → execution → monitoring.
support: Implied by book's structure and emphasis on end-to-end workflow
mechanism: Modularity enables independent validation, reuse, and debugging
validation: Design review and integration testing; measure deployment time and maintenance effort
